mcqs.q: A structure that allows X-rays to pass through and appears dark/black is termed:
mcqs.explain: Less dense structures let more x-rays through and appear dark — radiolucent (e.g. cavities, sinus, canal, foramen).

mcqs.q: Bony/dense structures that absorb X-rays appear ___ on a radiograph:
mcqs.explain: Dense, bony structures absorb x-rays and appear radiopaque (white).

mcqs.q: Which dental tissue is the MOST radiopaque?
mcqs.explain: Enamel is the densest/hardest tissue (96% inorganic), causing the greatest attenuation and appearing most radiopaque.
Dentin (~65% inorganic) is less radiopaque than enamel.

mcqs.q: The pulp cavity on a radiograph appears:
mcqs.explain: The pulp chamber and root canal contain soft tissue and appear radiolucent.

mcqs.q: Cementum is usually NOT apparent on a radiograph because it is:
opts: Thin and has very low contrast against dentin
mcqs.explain: Cementum is thin and the contrast between it and dentin is very low, so it is not radiographically apparent.

mcqs.q: The lamina dura corresponds to which structure?
opts: The outer layer of dense cortical bone lining the socket
The basal bone of the jaw
The buccal and lingual cortical plates
mcqs.explain: The lamina dura is the thin, dense radiopaque cortical bone lining the socket; it gives attachment to the principal PDL fibres.

mcqs.q: An intact lamina dura around a tooth apex usually indicates:
mcqs.explain: An intact lamina dura around the apex suggests a vital pulp; loss of the apical lamina dura suggests a periapical abscess.

mcqs.q: Loss of the lamina dura around the apex suggests:
mcqs.explain: Loss of the apical lamina dura is associated with periapical pathology such as a periapical abscess.

mcqs.q: Rounding of the alveolar crest (loss of its sharp angle) indicates:
mcqs.explain: The alveolar crest normally forms a sharp angle continuous with the lamina dura; rounding indicates periodontal disease.

mcqs.q: On a radiograph, cancellous (spongy) bone shows:
opts: Radiopaque trabeculae with radiolucent marrow spaces
A solid radiopaque mass with no spaces
mcqs.explain: Cancellous bone is made of radiopaque trabeculae with intervening radiolucent medullary (marrow) spaces.

mcqs.q: The PDL space on a radiograph is a radiolucent line that is:
opts: Widest coronally and slightly narrower at the apex
mcqs.explain: The PDL space (mainly collagen) appears as a radiolucent line between root and lamina dura, widest coronally.

mcqs.q: Loss of the PDL space (the tooth fused to bone) indicates:
mcqs.explain: Loss of the radiolucent PDL space indicates ankylosis (fusion of the tooth to the surrounding bone).

mcqs.q: Cortical bone produces no image normally but is identifiable as radiopaque at the:
opts: Inferior border of the mandible, alveolar crest and sinus/palate borders
mcqs.explain: Cortical bone is identifiable as radiopaque at the inferior border of the mandible, the alveolar crest between teeth, and the cortical borders of the hard palate and sinus.

mcqs.q: In the posterior mandible, the trabecular bone pattern typically appears as a:
mcqs.explain: The posterior mandible typically shows a stepladder trabecular pattern; the anterior mandible shows a horizontal pattern with larger marrow spaces.

mcqs.q: Trabecular bone (and any bone) on a radiograph is:
mcqs.explain: Bone trabeculae are radiopaque; the marrow spaces between them are radiolucent.

mcqs.q: The anterior maxilla typically shows trabeculae that are:
opts: Thin and numerous, with small numerous marrow spaces
mcqs.explain: The anterior maxilla has thin, numerous trabeculae with small, numerous marrow spaces; posteriorly the marrow spaces are larger.

mcqs.q: The alveolar process is best defined as:
opts: The part of the maxilla/mandible that forms and supports the tooth sockets
The enamel covering of the crown
mcqs.explain: The alveolar process is the part of the maxilla or mandible that forms and supports the sockets of the teeth.

saqs.a: Radiolucent = less dense, lets x-rays pass → dark/black. Radiopaque = dense/bony, absorbs x-rays → white.

saqs.q: Rank enamel, dentin and pulp by radiographic density.
saqs.a: Enamel = most radiopaque (96% inorganic) > dentin (65%, less radiopaque) > pulp cavity = radiolucent. (Cementum is not apparent.)

saqs.q: What is the lamina dura and its clinical importance?
saqs.a: A dense radiopaque cortical layer lining the socket (PDL attachment). Intact around the apex = vital pulp; loss = periapical abscess.

saqs.q: Describe the radiographic appearance of cancellous bone.
Why is cementum not seen on a radiograph?
saqs.a: It is too thin and the contrast between cementum and dentin is very low.

saqs.q: Give the radiographic signs of (a) PDL disease and (b) ankylosis.
saqs.a: (a) Rounding of the alveolar crest; (b) loss of the PDL space.
